clinicalPearls: The mediastinum lies between the pleural sacs, bounded superiorly by the thoracic inlet and inferiorly by the diaphragm, and is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments, each prone to characteristic lesions.
Localizing a mediastinal mass to one of the three compartments is the essential first diagnostic step, since each compartment harbors a distinct set of typical lesions.

The anterior compartment is the source of thymomas, germ cell tumors (including teratomas), lymphomas, and thyroid goiter; thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal neoplasm and is closely linked to paraneoplastic syndromes, most notably myasthenia gravis.
Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies in serum support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis in the setting of an anterior mediastinal mass.

Teratomas are the most common germ cell tumor and appear as multilobulated cystic lesions containing fat, soft tissue, and calcium; elevated alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG distinguish nonseminomatous from seminomatous germ cell tumors.

Most middle mediastinal masses are benign and developmental in origin, including bronchogenic cysts (abnormal ventral foregut budding), duplication cysts (persistent dorsal foregut diverticulum), and pericardial cysts (abnormal pericardial recess fusion).
Neurogenic tumors are the most common cause of posterior mediastinal masses and are frequently benign, arising from peripheral, autonomic, or paraganglionic nervous tissue.

Superior vena cava syndrome is a medical emergency presenting with severe dyspnea and facial/upper-extremity edema; malignancy causes most cases, with lung cancer (especially small-cell carcinoma) accounting for up to 50%.
Acute mediastinitis most often follows esophageal perforation, median sternotomy for cardiac surgery, or infection descending from the neck, oral cavity, or face.

Hamman's sign — a crunching/clicking sound synchronous with the heartbeat, best heard over the anterior chest in the left lateral decubitus position — together with suprasternal subcutaneous emphysema suggests pneumomediastinum.
Most fibrosing mediastinitis follows prior granulomatous infection, commonly histoplasmosis or tuberculosis, though sarcoidosis, silicosis, and fungal disease may also be causative.
Barium gastrointestinal studies are useful in many posterior mediastinal lesions because hernias, diverticula, and achalasia are readily identified this way.
harrison.pathophysiology: Disorders of the mediastinum arise from the anatomical structures of its three compartments. Anterior compartment lesions stem from the thymus, lymph nodes, germinal/thyroid tissue, and mammary vessels, giving rise to thymomas, germ cell tumors, lymphomas, and goiter. Middle compartment disease typically reflects embryologic developmental abnormalities producing foregut-derived cysts (bronchogenic, duplication, pericardial), or malignant lymphadenopathy and vascular masses; because central vasculature resides here, compression of structures such as the SVC can produce acute life-threatening physiology. Posterior compartment lesions are predominantly neurogenic, with contributions from diaphragmatic hernia, meningocele, esophageal diverticula, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Acute mediastinitis is an inflammatory/infectious process driven by esophageal breach, post-sternotomy wound contamination, or descending cervicofacial infection. Chronic and fibrosing mediastinitis represents a spectrum from granulomatous lymph node inflammation to dense fibrosis, usually following granulomatous infection, with progressive encasement and obstruction of mediastinal structures (SVC, large airways, pulmonary vessels, phrenic/recurrent laryngeal nerves). Pneumomediastinum results from alveolar rupture with air dissection into the mediastinum, perforation/rupture of esophagus or airway, or dissection of air from the neck or abdomen.
additionalDifferentials: Germ cell tumors / teratoma (seminomatous and nonseminomatous)
Parathyroid and mesenchymal tumors; giant lymph node hyperplasia
Metastatic and granulomatous lymph node enlargement; vascular masses
Neurogenic tumors, meningocele/meningomyelocele, gastroenteric cysts, esophageal diverticula, extramedullary hematopoiesis, hernia through foramen of Morgagni or Bochdalek
infectionMimics: Granulomatous mediastinitis from histoplasmosis or tuberculosis
Descending cervicofacial/oropharyngeal infection involving the mediastinum
nonInfectiousMimics: Lymphoma presenting as anterior/middle mediastinal lymphadenopathy
Sarcoidosis and silicosis causing fibrosing mediastinitis
Vascular masses and aortic pathology widening the mediastinum
additionalInvestigations: CT scanning to characterize fat, water, calcification, and air within mediastinal masses
Diffusion-weighted MRI to differentiate cystic from solid lesions and improve tumor characterization
Mediastinoscopy for sampling of paratracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes
Percutaneous fine-needle aspiration or endoscopic transesophageal/endobronchial ultrasound biopsy
Radioactive iodine scintigraphy to confirm intrathoracic goiter
Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG for germ cell tumor classification; serum anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies when thymoma/myasthenia is suspected
Barium GI studies for posterior mediastinal lesions (hernia, diverticulum, achalasia)
Mediastinal needle aspiration to confirm post-sternotomy mediastinitis
Chest radiograph to confirm pneumomediastinum; tissue biopsy in fibrosing mediastinitis to exclude malignancy
redFlags: Superior vena cava syndrome (severe dyspnea, facial and upper-extremity edema) — a medical emergency
Acutely ill patient with chest pain and dyspnea suggesting esophageal rupture with mediastinal infection
Post-sternotomy wound drainage with sepsis and a widened mediastinum
Severe substernal chest pain radiating to neck/arms with subcutaneous emphysema (pneumomediastinum)
Hemoptysis, dysphagia, or Horner's syndrome in fibrosing mediastinitis indicating structural invasion/obstruction
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying disorder. Most middle mediastinal masses and posterior neurogenic tumors are benign. Anterior mediastinal neoplasms vary widely, and disease severity across mediastinal masses spans a broad spectrum; clinical symptoms, patient age, and tumor location guide assessment of malignancy and need for intervention. Acute post-sternotomy mediastinitis carries a mortality rate exceeding 20% despite treatment. Fibrosing mediastinitis can be devastating in severe cases owing to obstruction/encasement of vital structures. Pneumomediastinum usually requires no treatment and resolves with absorption of air.
pitfalls: Failing to compartmentalize a mediastinal mass before working it up, since each compartment has different characteristic lesions.
Overlooking that advanced malignancy may not remain confined to one compartment and can cross borders via hematogenous and lymphatic spread.
Underappreciating SVC compression in the middle mediastinum as an acute, life-threatening emergency.
Missing the link between an anterior mediastinal mass (thymoma) and paraneoplastic myasthenia gravis.
Assuming fibrosing mediastinitis is purely structural without recognizing its common antecedent granulomatous infection and need to exclude malignancy by biopsy.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading system; mediastinal disorders are stratified anatomically into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments, and severity is judged by clinical symptoms, patient age, lesion location, likelihood of malignancy, and presence of acute complications such as SVC obstruction or airway compromise.
